subject: neonAlley
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: rainy neon alleyway with noodle shop.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
For the diorama, I want to avoid the obvious cyberpunk neon route and pick something more unexpected — maybe a paper-cut shadowbox theater look with layered cardboard flats and a riso two-ink palette, or alternatively a 3D ukiyo-e woodblock print aesthetic.

I'll commit to a "neon ukiyo-e" direction, channeling Hiroshige's rain prints but swapping in glowing neon kanji signage, flat indigo/vermilion/bone tones, hatched rain lines, and sumi ink outlines, built on a shallow tray base with alley walls rising from it. Since this is a static model I don't need joints, so I'll build everything with plain parts positioned via coordinates rather than bone attachments. I'm sizing the diorama as a miniature scene, roughly a meter wide by over a meter deep, and now thinking through how the alley should be laid out within that footprint before writing the module itself.

I'm laying out the alley scene: a base slab roughly 1.2 by 1.6 units with buildings rising on either side of a 0.6-wide gap, a back wall closing the far end with a glowing distant sign, and a noodle shop tucked on the left with an awning, counter, stools, steam, a lantern, and neon signage. For the wet street I'm planning glowing flat decals to suggest neon reflected in puddles, and for rain I'm considering scattering thin card geometry with a streak texture across the scene to read as falling rain.

Now I'm refining the rain cards: small tapering rectangles sized around 0.012 by 0.16, scattered randomly in the open alley column and above the rooftops, tilted along a slanted axis so they read as diagonal rain streaks like in ukiyo-e prints, facing the viewer with both sides visible, with roughly 220 cards total. I'm deciding on color -- pale cyan-white streaks against the dark indigo night, possibly mixing in some darker streaks for variation.

For the ink-outline look, I'm weighing cheap tricks: adding thin edge rods along box boundaries for the main structures, or finding a way to darken edges within the box material itself since a larger dark box behind wouldn't produce a visible outline.

I'm sketching a border-darkening scheme using UV proximity—edges near u or v extremes get darkened—then checking texel density against a shared paint atlas to make sure thin borders stay crisp, settling on a larger 2048px paint sheet for better resolution.

Now I'm defining a reusable wood-block paint helper that layers grain texture with edge darkening.

For the wall surfaces I want a bokashi-style gradient, subtly darker toward the top like Hiroshige's sky bands, combined with gentle wood-grain noise variation. To get accurate edge outlines per face, I'm deriving face dimensions from the surface normal direction, then computing edge distance using those dimensions inside the paint closure.

Windows and other detailed elements get separate textured planes layered on top. For the palette I'm settling on a Hiroshige night-rain scheme — deep indigo sumi ink, prussian blue walls, aged plaster tones, dark wood, vermilion accents, and neon pink/cyan glows for modern contrast.

Now I'm working out the spatial orientation carefully, figuring out which side the noodle shop sits on relative to the viewer's perspective and the model's coordinate axes so the scene reads correctly from the camera's viewpoint.

Buildings form an open-fronted diorama block cut at the front edge, so the viewer looks down the alley: glowing shop facade on the left, signboards on the right building, and a neon street visible through the back arch. Now I'm working out the dimension plan in meters, starting with the base tray box.

Since the lowest point needs to touch the floor at y=0, I'm keeping the base as a simple box with an inked wooden-frame edge rather than a lathed shape, possibly with a thin label strip on the front face. Rendering actual CJK text is risky given font availability, so I'm considering drawing pseudo-kanji using hand-built SVG stroke paths instead of relying on system fonts.

I'm settling on using katakana ラメン (ramen) built from a few simple stroke shapes, since it's visually simpler than full kanji while still reading authentically as a noodle-shop sign.

Drawing katakana strokes...

Still drafting glyph strokes...

Now I'm planning the overall composition: stacking the three katakana glyphs vertically into a neon sign viewBox, then designing the glow effect with pink strokes and white cores set against a dark backing board.

For the base layer, I'm figuring out the street surface—wet cobblestones rendered with scattered dark indigo tiles, plus puddle zones marked by noise thresholds that get a pale reflective color with streaky neon reflections layered on top as separate glowing discs.

Writing puddle disc geometry...

Now I'm laying out the left-side buildings: a noodle shop with an open counter facing +X, ground floor around 0.42 height, and an upper floor box stacked above it from roughly y=0.47 to 0.77.

The ground floor needs a sloped tile roof overhang, dark indigo with tile texture, plus a glowing amber interior showing a cook silhouette, shelves, and bowls to sell the depth. Since the camera views the alley obliquely, both the shop's +X-facing front and the opposite building's -X-facing facade get foreshortened, which is the classic alley look I want to capture.

Now I'm laying out the shop's shell geometry: back wall, floor, side walls positioned along the z-axis, with the front open between certain z-bounds and a counter box jutting slightly into the alley at a set height.

For the noren curtains hanging from the beam, I'm planning a textured plane facing outward with four indigo panels bearing a white emblem and slit gaps for a traditional shop-curtain look, positioned over the upper part of the opening above the counter.

I'm also filling out the scene with a warm emissive back wall, bottle shelves, a cook figure with a hachimaki headband, a steaming stockpot with soft puff-textured steam cards, bowls of noodles with narutomaki and egg, three-legged stools in the alley, and a seated customer holding a ribbed wagasa umbrella to echo the classic ukiyo-e imagery.

I'm scrapping the seated customer idea in favor of a walking figure holding a large red umbrella in the alley — an indigo-striped kimono with obi sash, a hair bun, geta sandals, and the umbrella built as a lathe shape with painted ribs drawn procedurally by sector angle. I'm also adding hanging red chōchin lanterns with ribbed paint, black caps, and kanji decal strokes above the scene.

Now I'm planning the upper floor with glowing shoji windows showing warm silhouettes, and working out the roof as an extruded gable profile with curved eaves and tiled paint, overhanging toward the alley.

On the right side, I'm sketching a taller three-story izakaya/apartment building with a window grid, AC units, exposed pipes, a fire escape, jutting neon signs, and a shuttered ground-floor shop with a glowing vending machine as a key neon detail.

I'm adding sagging catenary wires strung from a utility pole with transformer across the alley to the buildings, water tanks on stilts atop the right building's setback roofline, and merged balcony railings. On the left I'm placing another tall narrow building with a bold vertical "BAR" neon sign, and behind it all a painted backdrop plane showing a distant glowing street scene to give depth.

Now I'm designing that backdrop as an indigo-to-plum gradient sky with bokashi shading, lit windows, and a pale glowing moon disc in ukiyo-e style rather than a full moon since it's raining, sizing the panel to frame the alley and keeping its emissive glow modest so it doesn't wash out. I'm also adding a vermillion cartouche with a seal and glyph-like text to the base's front face as a decorative ukiyo-e title element.

I'm thinking about triangle and part budgets—keeping boxes cheap and cards low-poly, aiming for roughly 250 parts total, and setting up a compact builder helper. I need to watch the color-string limit since flat colors count against it while textures and paints don't, so I'm leaning on painted parts to stay under that cap while writing a reusable box helper for the geometry.

I'm reasoning through paint costs: each inked box bakes its own chart on a shared 2048 paint sheet, so with ~100 painted boxes the texel density stays fine around 1.6mm, but to keep things efficient I'll only use the inked paint treatment on the ~40 primary structural pieces and use plain flat-color boxes for smaller details without outlines.

Writing wood-block paint helper...

Adding woodblock grain shading...

Still tuning the noise scaling...

I want to stretch the noise vertically for vein-like streaks by scaling x and z more than y, then use that as a subtle darkening factor on box faces, and confirm the uv and noise/paint helpers are properly exported from the SDK's index file.

I'm settling on a set of textures to build out, aiming for 5-12 total: a neon ramen sign, a shop curtain, puddle reflections, rain streak cards, steam puffs, a shoji window lattice with warm glow, a city backdrop, and a vending machine front with rows of cans, among others.

For lanterns, I'm deciding to keep it simple rather than full kanji glyphs — maybe a plane with black glyph strokes placed slightly outside the lantern surface to suggest text without overcomplicating the geometry.

Then I'm sketching out remaining smaller details: a vertical neon sign on the right building, the cartouche within the backdrop, and the noodle bowl's top surface with swirls, naruto, egg, nori, and scallions, acknowledging these are tiny but worth a touch of texture.

Adding a hanging wooden menu board with price-list style strokes and red circles for the noodle shop, then deciding not to overdo the details and starting to write each texture as its own compact function. Now I'm defining ink-stroke glyph paths for pseudo-characters...

Writing glyph scaling function...

For the sign geometry itself, I'm deciding between a thin box with the texture on all faces (edges would smear) versus a dark flat body box with a separate textured plane overlay for cleaner edges, leaning toward the layered approach to avoid stretching artifacts on the sides.

For the puddle texture, I'm designing an ellipse with dark blue fill and ink stroke, a paler sky-blue inner ellipse, and colored wavy reflection strokes in pink, cyan, and amber, plus ripple circles to suggest raindrops—keeping the shape centered so it maps cleanly onto the circular disc crop.

I'm working through how to use CircleGeometry with a low facet count for the puddle, non-uniformly scaled to look elliptical, while lifting it slightly to avoid z-fighting with the street plane. Now I'm sketching the rain streak card texture as a thin tapered polygon shape.

Choosing pale blue-lavender lines for the rain against the dark background, and sketching a steam puff card next—overlapping ink-outlined circles in a paper tone, styled like ukiyo-e clouds, with cards stacked to suggest steam rising from a pot facing frontward.

Now I'm planning the backdrop texture: a tall gradient sky fading from deep indigo to purple-pink near the horizon, with brush-stroke rain bands, silhouetted buildings with lit amber windows, a distant tower with red lights, neon glow, and diagonal rain streaks layered across the whole scene.

Designing the window texture with warm lattice glow and a seated silhouette, then the vending machine texture with glowing can rows and buttons, and starting on the noren curtain texture...

Working out the orientation math for the noren panel facing +X: since the viewer stands at +X looking back toward -X, their right side corresponds to -Z, so left-to-right reading order on the fabric maps to high-Z to low-Z in world space. I'll just order the glyphs in the SVG accordingly so they read correctly from the alley view.

For the shop interior, I'm simplifying the bowls to flat-color lathe shapes—pale yellow noodle discs, white-and-pink naruto spirals, and sphere egg halves—kept tiny at roughly 0.025 radius and placed along the counter. I'm also scaling the whole scene so the 0.33m-tall opening and a human figure sized around 0.28m stay proportionate to a roughly 1:6 scale alley.

Now I'm working out the vertical layout: ground floor from y=0.05 to 0.45, counter top around 0.22, stools near 0.09 high, and the cook positioned behind the counter so the noren curtain hangs just above their head without covering it. I'm then stacking the upper floor from 0.45 to 0.75 with a slight overhang toward the alley and placing the roof eave at the top.

I'm sketching the roof peak at 0.9 for the left shop (total height 0.9) versus 1.2 for the right building, with the alley kept at 0.6 wide. The shop's depth along the alley runs from z=0.12 to 0.8. Behind it, I'm planning a 3-floor bar/hotel structure with a window grid, a vertical "BAR" neon sign, AC units, and a pipe, while the right building splits into two volumes — a 2-storey izakaya in front with lantern strings, a sliding entrance door, and a vending machine near the ground.

Now I'm defining helper functions for constructing boxes by corner coordinates and color, considering how to type the color parameter and whether to specify a box by its center or by min/max corners, setting up a `blk` helper that takes explicit x/y/z ranges plus color and an inking option.

I'm also working out how to build the gabled roof shapes, defining a profile of points across the cross-section for the shop roof with overhangs, ridge height, and eave positioning to extrude along the building's length.

Still shaping the gable roof outline...

I'm thinking the roof gets a dark grey-blue base with pale wet highlights on upward-facing surfaces, plus a neon spill effect that tints rooftops pink or cyan based on proximity to the shop sign.

I'm posterizing the light falloff into discrete bands for that woodblock bokashi look, and setting up a global lights array so the spill function can tint any surface based on distance and normal direction, starting with a pink sign light placed to the left.

Now I'm placing the remaining lights: a warm amber shop lantern, a pink neon ramen sign, a cyan BAR sign on the right building, and a white-cyan vending machine glow, each with its own radius and falloff color, then applying this tint function across all the inkPaint surfaces including the wet street with its upward-facing light reflections.

Writing street paint shader...

I'm using the cells function to generate cobblestone cracks with a dark base color varying per cell id, then tinting with the street lights. I'm adding a darker central drain gutter line and letting wet puddle reflections pick up the colored neon streaks, before defining the tray base as a dark wood box with inked edges around the whole scene.

Now I'm working out the tray geometry — deciding whether the street surface is just the top face of the tray or a separate inset slab, and sketching a thin raised wood rim to frame the street area at the correct height.

I'll skip the plaque idea and put the cartouche in the backdrop instead, with the street extending to the open front end at z=0.85. Now I'm setting up the shared code skeleton, importing the builder utilities and glow kit needed for each section.

I'm deciding to avoid geometry merging since part counts stay well under budget, and I'm planning to use faceted cylinders for a low-poly look, working through rotation parameters next.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for cylinders and connecting rods between two points, with options for radius, color, and faceted sides to keep the geometry stylized rather than smooth.

Then I'm thinking through sagging wire paths using Catmull-Rom sweeps for a hand-drawn feel, and designing lantern shapes with lathe profiles that curve outward from the central axis.

Since painted surfaces can't glow, I realize the lantern needs a separate glowing part with a flat color material layered beneath the painted rib details.

I'll add optional glyph decals as dark ink strokes on larger lanterns, keeping decals non-glowing while the lantern body stays lit. Now I'm scaling down scope and starting to write the actual implementation code.

Setting up palette constants...

Writing the lighting blend function...

Still writing paint function...

I'm building the tray and street boxes with layered wood and street paint, positioning the street surface slightly above the tray rim, then starting to lay out puddle positions along the alley.

Each puddle uses a scaled circle geometry oriented flat against the street, with the x and z radii mapped into the mesh's local scale so they stretch into proper puddle shapes rather than perfect circles.

For the backdrop, I'm positioning a plane at the rear of the diorama with a thin wooden shadowbox frame just behind it, offsetting the frame slightly deeper in z to simulate depth around the scene.

I'm writing an SVG gradient for the backdrop sky, transitioning from deep night blues through purples to a warm pink-amber glow near the horizon, mimicking distant city light pollution over the street.

For cloud bands and distant buildings, I'm using a deterministic random function to generate silhouettes—dark rectangles with lit amber windows scattered across nine buildings of varying heights along the 124-unit width, giving the backdrop depth and realism.

In the alley-end opening between the side buildings, I'm adding a central tower with a red beacon and glowing pink/cyan signage, plus diagonal rain streaks rendered as thin light-blue paths for atmosphere. I'm also placing a vermilion cartouche in the top-right corner with a white glyph stroke and seal detail.

I need to check the vertical scale so the cartouche sits above the right-side building rather than being occluded by it—mapping the plane's height range so the cartouche's svg y-coordinates stay clear of the building's 1.2m height line.

Now I'm setting building heights (right ~1.15, left ~1.05) and starting the left shop geometry: defining the floor slab with wooden boards and the amber-lit back wall to suggest warm interior lighting from a lantern.

Adding an interior light point plus shelves with bottles, then laying out the side walls, ceiling slab, and front header beam with their dimensions and materials.

Now I'm planning the dark wood pillars flanking the side walls, then the wooden counter with its top slab and a vermilion-striped apron, followed by positioning a noren curtain plane just in front of the beam.

Next I'm sketching the cook figure standing behind the counter -- a white apron cylinder body, skin-toned head sphere, headband, and tiny eye dots -- working out proportions so the torso and arms reach forward toward the pot without making the figure too short.

Then I'm placing the steaming pot on the stove counter, a small cylinder for the body with an open top, sized so it reads clearly between the counter and the hanging noren curtain.

Adding bowls to the counter now, lathing their profiles with closed loops from axis out and back, and placing a noodle disc on top with a warm tan color.

Then I'm layering in the small details: a naruto disc, egg half, scallion bits, nori strip, red bowl body with an ink rim, and steam cards rising. For the stools, I'm placing three along x=-0.19 with cylindrical tops and ink-rimmed vermilion coloring, plus legs and a seated customer.

For the customer, I'm building a hunched figure wearing an indigo torso, a sphere head, and a conical straw kasa hat, facing the counter with simplified thigh and shin boxes for the seated pose. I'm skipping a separate menu board for now and considering whether to add a hanging price sign near the entrance.

Instead I'm focusing on the upper floor facade, building the plaster box and planning shoji window planes with dark wooden frame boxes mounted on the front face to suggest traditional mullions.

Working out the hisashi slab profile coordinates so it sits above the beam without blocking the noren view, then moving on to defining the shop's gable roof shape along the z-axis.

Still refining the roof polygon...

Still working out curve points...

Now I'm placing the hanging lanterns — two red chochin flanking the shop beam ends near the hisashi overhang, plus considering a string of smaller lanterns strung across the alley toward the building opposite.

I'm figuring out a sagging wire path for the lantern string, spacing mini lanterns along a curve between the two buildings using a frame-generating helper that walks the path and positions each lantern slightly below it.

Now I'm placing a vertical neon shop sign projecting from the wall near the front corner, sizing its box and positioning the textured faces so it's visible face-on from the viewer's angle.

I'll skip extra signage for simplicity, instead adding an interior back-wall shelf with colored bottle cylinders and a bare hanging bulb with warm glow near the shop's rear corner, then move on to the left rear building.

Now I'm designing the hotel/bar building spanning that back-left footprint, with a ground-floor storefront using dark shutters and a vermilion door, plus three upper floors of windows alternating between warm lit shoji-style panels and dark indigo glass with a diagonal reflection streak, arranged in a repeating grid across the wall's depth.

I'm placing ledge boxes beneath each window, scattering some AC units with grills, and running a steel drain pipe vertically along one corner from roof to ground. Then I'm adding a tall cyan neon "BAR" sign projecting from the wall, built from glowing planes with stacked Latin lettering rendered in a bold sans-serif font.

For the roof I'm adding a parapet, water tank, and antenna. The right building front gets two floors with an izakaya-style entrance, an amber-glowing sliding door, a vending machine, shoji-lit upper windows, a corrugated flat roof, and a hanging "酒" lantern sign. The right rear section gets four floors of apartments with balcony slabs and railings, a zigzagging exterior fire escape leading to the roof, more AC units, and another water tank, with the small gap between the front and rear sections closed off so the building reads as one continuous wall.

Now I'm placing a wooden utility pole in the alley near the vending machine, with a crossarm, transformer cylinder, and four sweeping wires connecting to the buildings. For the umbrella figure, I'm positioning it mid-alley walking away from the viewer so we see the back of the kimono and obi bow, scaled to about 0.28m tall, starting with simple geta sandal shapes and a lathed kimono skirt profile.

I'm adding indigo kimono fabric with pale vertical stripes based on angular position, a vermilion obi band with a back bow, a small head with black hair, bun, and kanzashi ornament, and an umbrella shaft rising from the figure's hand.

Still shaping the umbrella profile...

I'm adding a snake-eye pattern with a white ring near the vermilion rim, and considering a slight tilt for the umbrella. I'm also thinking about adding a small black cat with glowing eyes sitting on a crate near the dumpster, built from scaled body and head spheres.

Now I'm detailing the cat further with ear cones, a tail sweep, and tiny glowing yellow eyes, placing it on a stack of yellow beer crates. I'm also considering adding a parked bicycle leaning against the right wall using torus wheels and frame rods for recognizable primitive shapes.

Finishing the bicycle's wheels, spokes, hub, and frame tubes, then sketching overhead wires from the pole and sorting out the color scheme for the right building's front block.

Settling on warm wooden shopfront tones with plaster upper levels, and varying the palette across buildings for contrast—indigo night sky against left shop plaster, prussian blue rear building, and a brick-red right front with glass door, lanterns, noren, and a vending machine to add.

Working out the vending machine's facing texture plane, its position and orientation on the -X facing wall, then placing the upper-story shoji windows along the right facade.

For the right rear section, I'm laying out floor heights and window grids across four stories, then considering whether to add balcony slabs or convert that into a fire escape with landings running down the side.

Now I'm building the fire escape itself: steel landing slabs with railing posts and rails, plus diagonal stairs made from small tread boxes between stringer rods, repeated across three flights. I'm mirroring the same window pattern for the left rear facade, and sanity-checking that part and triangle counts stay well under budget given low-segment cylinders. Now I'm writing the window helper function...

For rain cards, I'm setting up the slanted axis so the flow direction flattens mostly along -z, meaning card width runs perpendicular along x, keeping them visible from the front.

I'm also figuring out rain placement with random x/z/y bounds while adding a rule to exclude positions that'd fall inside building geometry, checking roof heights on each side.

I'm considering whether to add splash rings in puddles or skip them, and thinking about whether to add a wavy ukiyo-e style cloud band near the top of the alley for atmosphere.

Now I'm working out how to draw a steam puff using three overlapping circles with ink outlines, layering stroked and filled versions to create a clean unioned silhouette without internal lines showing through.

Then I move to card placement details—sizing, orientation, and flow direction for the cards—before starting on the neon ramen bowl texture, sketching its SVG viewBox and the outer rounded rectangle with a pink stroke border.

Writing double-stroke outline and glyph layout...

Actually, let me pivot to a noren (shop curtain) design instead: four hanging panels in indigo with white ramen-related glyphs (katakana strokes, a mon circle) centered in each, plus a top hanging bar and thin cut slits between panels.

For a shoji screen piece, I'm setting up a radial amber gradient background with a wooden lattice overlay, then adding a simple dark silhouette of a figure—a head, shoulders, and a hair bun—behind the screen.

Still designing textures... now sketching a vending machine with rows of cans, a coin slot, and a dark outlet panel, plus lantern glyph decals using simple ink strokes on transparent backgrounds.

I'm tallying up the texture count — neon signs, noren, shoji panels, puddle, rain, steam, lantern glyphs — landing around thirteen, slightly over my soft target but acceptable. Now I'm thinking through how to orient the glyph decals on the lantern surfaces, positioning them at specific points with a defined facing direction.

For the shop lanterns I'll place decals facing the viewer along the z-axis, offset slightly from the lantern center, using small sizing and segment counts since the glow material won't make the ink glyphs glow themselves. I'm also working out how the seeded RNG function is meant to be called based on its documented signature.

I'm checking the signatures for placing cards along frames, scattering objects along a catmull path with callbacks, and applying glow wrappers to parts, plus confirming there's no GLB size limit. I'm also looking at how the lathe function handles outlines, smoothing creases above a threshold angle, and segment counts for rounded shapes like bowls.

Now I'm nailing down extrude options and torus orientation—rotating a torus 90° on the x-axis for a horizontal ring versus 90° on the y-axis for a vertical wheel—before writing strict TypeScript with underscore-prefixed unused params and a tuple type for vectors. Setting up the overall code structure with a neon-themed style comment...

Writing imports and type definitions...

Adding more light positions...

Still writing street paint logic...

Still writing helper functions...

Defining the lantern geometry profile...

Adding caps, rings, and glyph decal...

I'm adding a small tassel cone below the lantern and setting the glow to a bright vermilion red. Then I'm defining a smaller lantern variant for string decorations and starting the kimono paint function, which stripes the surface by angle into alternating pale and deep blue bands with a hem pattern near the bottom.

Now I'm working out the umbrella's paint logic, radial ribs in ink color with a pale janome ring near the rim and red elsewhere, then checking the lathe angle parameter before moving to the cat's body shape using a scaled sphere. I'm mindful of keeping the code concise as I write the remaining pieces in full.

Setting up builder helpers...

Smooth should override shading as expected, and static models can skip joints entirely since rods work fine with plain endpoint arrays and no bones. I'm double-checking that the plane geometry's axis and direction settings align correctly.

Now I'm defining the glyph stroke paths as SVG path data for each character, building out the texture constants at module level...

Adding glyph outlines for the ramen text with layered pink and white strokes...

Now I'm sketching the NOREN panel design with a top bar, four hanging panels, and a hem for the shop curtain emblem.

Still writing puddle reflections...

Now I'm designing a raindrop shape as a tapered polygon, pointed at the top and widest toward the bottom where it falls, then moving on to a backdrop built with deterministic pseudo-randomness.

Writing SVG gradient background...

Adding lit windows to each building, a street-level band with umbrella silhouettes for pedestrians, and a tall center tower topped with a vermilion beacon light.

Still writing cartouche glyphs...

I'm checking that the scale works out: the backdrop's longest side converts cleanly to pixels, and window proportions stay consistent. With the composition settled, I'm moving on to writing the full geometry code, starting with the tray and street base layers.

Now I'm placing the backdrop frame board and its front plane, checking that the z-offsets line up so the plane sits just in front of the board face without clipping into the tray geometry.

Checking frame border proportions, then defining puddle positions as coordinate-radius arrays scattered across the scene.

Scale applies before rotation, so that's fine. Now I'm setting up the noodle shop's floor, back wall, and side plaster walls using block primitives positioned to the left of the scene.

The side walls visible from outside stay plastered, and I'm adding an upper floor slab slightly overhanging at the front. For the back wall, I want it to feel warm and glowing like a lit kitchen, so I'm considering adding a separate glow plane with a gradient tint rather than just flat amber paint.

Setting that glow box with a warm orange tone, then placing shelves, bottles, and a cook silhouette in front as dark flat shapes against the lit wall for contrast, plus a ceiling bulb. Now I'm adding wooden header beams and pillars for the ground floor structure...

Then I'm building the counter with a darker wood base and lighter top surface, considering a vermilion apron stripe but deciding to skip it, and noting the counter faces the alley at an oblique angle to the viewer. Starting on a noren curtain plane next.

I need to make sure the noren hangs properly from the beam with the bottom edge positioned correctly, and the reading direction along the alley runs from +Z to -Z when viewed from +X. I'll handle the hisashi roof extrusion, cooking elements, and skip the wooden shop sign, then move to the pot, stove, and steam elements using frame-based positioning.

Now I'm working out the customer figure sitting on a stool facing the counter—placing the torso, head, kasa hat, thighs, shins, and feet with precise box and cylinder coordinates in indigo and skin tones.

Placing the arm reaching from shoulder to a bowl on the counter, checking the bowl fits within the counter top's x-range, then verifying the hat clears the noren and the stool height works with the thighs before moving on to the shoji window details above the shop front.

Still positioning windows and sign geometry...

I realize the sign position I picked actually collides with the hisashi eave structure, since the eave spans a y-range that overlaps the sign's bottom edge. I need to shift the sign higher, but then it risks hitting the roof overhang which only extends to x=-0.23, so I have to narrow the sign's horizontal placement to stay clear of that tip.

I'm shrinking the sign dimensions and recalculating its coordinates so it fits just above the hisashi top edge, accepting a tiny overlap near the roof corner as acceptable since the sign would appear mounted under the eave. Now I'm working out the extrusion parameters for the shop roof and hisashi, figuring out how the origin point and direction vectors determine the centering along the cross product axis.

Next I'm adding ridge cap details—a rod along the apex for the roof ridge and small box ornaments at the ends—then moving to the left rear building, setting its position and height range and giving it a deep blue body color. I'm also sketching out a ground-floor roll shutter as a flat grey panel with horizontal ridge lines built from thin boxes.

Now I'm fleshing out the storefront: a vermilion door box with an adjacent glowing amber window, then laying out floor levels with protruding ledge boxes and window positions at regular height bands, plus planning a few AC units mounted near the windows.

For the "BAR" sign, I'm working out its placement along the wall so it sits between windows rather than fully overlapping them, adjusting the z-coordinates of both the sign and the window columns to avoid collisions.

I'm settling on sign dimensions around width 0.15 and height 0.25, positioned to clear the alley space before moving on to design the roof parapet ring.

For the roof details, I'm adding a cylindrical water tank with legs and a cone lid, plus a drain pipe rod running down the side wall. Then I'm sketching out the right rear building with a cool lilac-grey body color and planning window placement by floor.

Now I'm working through the fire escape placement on this facade, figuring out landing positions at each floor level, window locations flanking the escape structure, and a door at one of the landings.

I'll simplify to a zigzag pattern: each flight runs steeply between landings with extended slabs at each floor level, using two stringer rods at slightly different x positions near the outer edge and wall.

Still working out the flight geometry...

Since the stairs cross the landing, I'll place windows only at specific z positions on the right rear wall, giving 3 windows across 4 floors for 12 total. The ground floor gets a shutter plane plus a doorway, and the roof needs a parapet with a classic wooden water tank on posts and some vents. For the right front block, I'm considering a brick lower section with plaster above.
